# greet

## Purpose and intended outcome

- Purpose: Create a tiny Node.js command-line tool that greets people.
- Intended outcome: A working command-line greeting tool, to be built under a later work item.

## Scope and boundaries

- In scope: The Node.js command-line greeting tool.
- Outside scope: Application code during project setup.
- Constraints: Build and test with Node.js; run tests with `node --test` (owner, 2026-09-27).

## Systems and environments

| System or org | Purpose | Environment | Source of truth | Access notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Local Node.js project | Command-line tool | Local development | This repository | No application code yet |

## People and ownership

| Role | Person or team | Responsibility | Source / last confirmed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | Mike | Project decisions and approvals | Owner, 2026-09-27 |

## Work and project records

- Work tracker: `.work-items/` local folders
- Project roadmap: [PROJECT-ROADMAP.md](PROJECT-ROADMAP.md)
- Project decisions: [DECISIONS.md](DECISIONS.md)
- Functional requirements: [requirements/](requirements/)
- Design home: `With its work item: local DESIGN.md or the external item's own record or attachments.`
- System Guide: `system-guide/` templates; no current system has been documented yet
- Local memory: `.memory/` (built-in memory, flat, Git-ignored, and usable as an Obsidian vault; the setup choice is in `.toolkit.json`)
- Memory backup or sync: No destination chosen yet

## Resources and project paths

- Tests and checks: `node --test` (verified; currently finds zero tests)
- Outside references: `ai-external-knowledge/INDEX.md`

## Operating conventions

No application code until Mike requests it as a work item (owner, 2026-09-27).
# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.
# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.
# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. There is no proposal inbox; hold an unanswered question in the conversation and continue independent work.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.
# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.
# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip this for small edits and quick lookups.
# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.
# Local Work-Item Folders

This project tracks work in local folders under `.work-items/`. The folder is
Git-ignored, lives in the main checkout, and is shared by every worktree. It is
not backed up by Git: `toolkit export` is the backup.

## An item is found by its ID, not its path

- An item is a folder holding a record, `WORK-ITEM.md`, and `DESIGN.md` when a
  design exists. The frontmatter `id` (for example `WI-001`) is the item's
  identity. The folder name and the file name may change.
- Refer to items by ID everywhere. Find an item's files with
  `toolkit work show <id> --path`. Never guess a path.
- Create items only with `toolkit work new`. It takes the next ID under a lock,
  so parallel sessions never pick the same one. IDs are never reused.

## The owner may move folders, and the agent adapts

- The owner may move, rename, nest, or group item folders by hand. That is
  normal. `toolkit work sync` finds every item again by its ID; the session
  hooks and every `toolkit work` command run it. Report what moved and continue.
  Use the `work-organize` skill to reconcile anything the sync reports as
  missing or duplicated.
- A record inside another item's folder is that item's sub-item: its `parent`
  follows its location. A plain folder with no record is a group and changes no
  parent.
- `archive/` is a reserved group. Items there are hidden from the briefing and
  from `toolkit work next`.
- Never move, group, archive, or rename items on your own initiative. When the
  owner asks, use `toolkit work move <id> --under <id|group|archive|root>`.

## What the tracker ignores, and what it generates

- Ignored: `work-item-template/`, any folder whose name starts with `_` or `.`,
  and any record whose title is still `<Work item title>`.
- Generated by `toolkit work sync`: `DASHBOARD.md`. State kept by `toolkit work`:
  `.toolkit-state.json` (the ID-to-path map and the highest ID used). Never edit
  either by hand.
- Change frontmatter fields (stage, status, parent, waiting on, approvals) only
  with `toolkit work` commands. Body sections may be edited directly or with
  `toolkit work edit`; the hook checks the record after each edit.
- Keep any other files the owner put in an item folder.

name: work-on
description: 'Starts, continues, or logs project work: finds or creates the work item, works out where it stands, and runs its next step through to a built result. Use when the owner asks to build, add, fix, or change something, says "keep going" or "continue", names an item, or wants an idea logged for later.'

# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: `../../references/conventions.md` (saving, section edits, history) and `../../references/trackers.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. No session briefing in this conversation: run the command below. Exit code 4 (no `.toolkit.json`): open `project-setup` and stop.
   `toolkit brief`
2. Find the item: the id the owner named, or a title in the list that matches the request. Two possible matches: ask one question naming both. No match: it is new. When `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` names the item, read its phase there too.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit work list`
3. Size a new request. A quick edit (one sitting, no choice for the owner, no behavior recorded in `requirements/`): do it and report it, with no item. "Later", "backlog", "park that": check the list for a duplicate, create the item, write the owner's words unchanged into Starting request, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop. Anything else: create it the same way and continue.
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Starting request" --set-file <file>`
4. A substantial goal whose item shows `delivery: not-offered`: open `work-delegate` first. Quick questions and small edits get no offer.
5. Route by where the item stands, using the item and the "Continue with" column of the lifecycle. Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` (or the risk calls for it): `work-requirements`. More than one reasonable way to build it and no approved design: `solution-design`. Too big for one build: `work-organize`. Stages 09 to 11: `work-check`. Stages 12 to 14: `work-finish`. `waiting_on: owner`: ask that one question first (`work-decide`) and keep working on anything it does not block. Say the route in one line ("WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements; opening work-requirements."). Never ask the owner which stage it is in.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
6. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases `P1`, `P2` and tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) from the design's "Build and verification plan", in the format in `references/planning.md`. Tracking setup (stage 07) only when needed: the item's branch and worktree `wi-<number>-<slug>`; in a Salesforce project, the item's folder in `delivery/deployment/` through `sf-component-tracker`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
7. Build (stage 08) on the item's own branch and worktree. With a team recorded by `work-delegate`: one `builder` agent per independent task, one writer per path. Tests go with each task. Tick a task only with evidence. A task whose "Done when" names the owner is a question for him (step 8). Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` on each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. When the owner is needed: add an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with "owner" as who decides, set the item waiting on the owner, keep working on tasks that do not depend on the answer, and tell him in one line. After his last answer, set it back to the agent (`../../references/conventions.md`, "Waiting on the owner").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. This skill never records approvals, Done, merges, or deploys.
10. Before stopping with work unfinished: Overview (Current position, Next action) and Notes > Resume here are current, one history note says what changed, and validation is clean.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "<what changed>"`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `builder`: one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed to one. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task.
- `researcher`: one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker`: a plan check after step 6, before the build, when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's "Build and verification plan", the Roadmap, and the Tasks, and ask for a plan check.
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Sizing a request

- **Quick edit, no item:** one sitting, no decision for the owner, and it does not change behavior recorded in `requirements/`. Examples: fix a typo, rename a variable, answer a question. Report what changed in one line.
- **Log only:** the owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or "log a bug". Create the item at `01-discovery`, fill Starting request with his exact words, and stop. Do not start the work.
- **Work item:** everything else. A request that grows past a quick edit while you work on it becomes an item then, with the owner's words as the Starting request.
- Types: pick the closest from the lifecycle's type list. `build` and `data-load` need approved requirements before stage 03 is passed; the CLI refuses otherwise.

## Routing notes

- The lifecycle's "Continue with" column is the default. The item's real state decides: for example, a `task` type item with no open choices can skip requirements approval and go straight to planning, with the reason in a history note.
- Stages may be skipped, repeated, or revisited. Record a short reason when a move is not obvious.
- A worktree whose branch is named `wi-<number>-<slug>` belongs to that item. The briefing says so. Work on that item there.
- Several items at once: recommend what can proceed independently, what depends on another outcome, and which decision would unblock the most work. See `references/planning.md`.
- `PROJECT-ROADMAP.md` holds the project's phases (`P01`) and deliverable-sized work units, each naming its work item ID; item detail stays in the tracker. A new item that is one of those units gets its ID written into the unit, saved with `publish-docs`. An item's own phases (`P1`) are a different thing and live in its Roadmap section.

## Never

- Never record an approval, Done, or a cancel here. Those belong to `work-requirements`, `solution-design`, `work-check`, `work-decide`, and `work-finish`.
- Never merge, deploy, or write production data.
- Never create a second tracker or a local copy of items kept in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.

Use when the owner says "grill me", "ask me questions", "what should it do", or "check the spec", changes a requirement, or requirements are missing.'

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: `../../references/conventions.md`. Interview and writing rules: `references/writing-requirements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it. Use discovery while the goal is being worked out, refinement once requirements are being written. Requirements already approved and no change asked: stop and open the skill the lifecycle's "Continue with" column names.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work new --title "<title>" --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
2. Before asking anything, read the item (Starting request, Agreed goal, `R-xx`, Open Questions) and look up what the project already knows, so no question repeats an answer.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit memory find "<topic>"`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal only after a yes.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --set-file <file>`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason. Push back when an answer works against the goal.
5. Write each answer into the item before the next question: `R-xx` blocks (Status Refining, required behavior, boundaries, acceptance check, decision record) and the Acceptance list. Anything unanswered becomes an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with who must answer; the item waits on the owner while one of his is open, and goes back to the agent when he answers the last one. Build ideas go under Notes > Solution options and considerations, never into requirements. A fact the owner cannot answer: brief a `researcher` agent.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` agent with the requirements text. Fix what it finds or turn it into questions. Change nothing without a yes.
8. Show a short summary and ask one line: "Do you approve these requirements?" and set the item waiting on the owner. Yes: first mark each approved `R-xx` Finalized with who approved it and when, then record the approval (the command adds its own history row), quote his words in one note, and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open. Not yet: it stays waiting on him.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note "Owner's words: <quote>"`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Check the item, then hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst`: the spec check in step 7. Paste in the Starting request, Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, the Acceptance list, and the open questions.
- `researcher`: one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Spec check findings

The analyst reports: missing pieces; places not explicit end to end; wording a builder could misread; build details inside requirements; drift from the Agreed goal; research or history in the wrong place. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words. The owner approves, edits, or dismisses each one. A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session. Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Notes

- "Grill me" means a deep interview: keep asking, one question at a time, until every branch that could change the result is covered. End with "What have we not touched that could change this?"
- The owner thinks out loud; let him. Save settled answers as they come; do not wait for the interview to end.
- Brainstorming methods from other plugins may run inside this skill. The answers still land in the work item.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue body's Requirements section as `../../references/trackers.md` says.
# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command.
  Do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a pipe, or a redirect. Codex matches its
  command rule against the plain command.
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. Report it that way.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The file holds the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row "| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |"
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Files for `--set-file` and `--body-file`: write the full new text to a file
  in a temporary folder outside the repository (make one with `mktemp -d`).
  Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
  file there confuses the design lookup.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |
| A lasting fact, preference, or lesson | Project memory, through `memory-save` | One record |

- Check the item and memory before asking the owner a question again.
- When sources disagree, keep the conflict open and ask. Do not pick the
  convenient answer.
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not
  approval. `toolkit work lifecycle` prints what counts as approval.
- Read the section back after saving. A command that exits `0` is not proof
  by itself.

## Reporting a failed save

- A write failed: lead with "Not saved", name what was not saved and where it
  should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- The write worked and the read-back failed: lead with "Saved but not
  verified".
- Never say "updated" first and correct it later in the same reply.

## When to add a history note

Add one `toolkit work history <id> --note "<text>"` when:

- the stage, type, priority, `waiting_on`, blockers, or next action changes
  for a reason that is not obvious;
- the owner gives a choice, an answer, a requirement, a constraint, an
  approval, or a rejection (quote his words);
- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you
  checked it);
- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

Record the owner's meaning briefly. Do not add reasons, scope, or certainty he
did not give. Do not log routine commands, files opened, ordinary test runs,
or small edits.

## Waiting on the owner

- Set `waiting_on` to `owner` when you ask the owner for an approval or add an
  Open Questions row that he must answer.
- `toolkit work approve` does not change `waiting_on`. After each recorded
  approval, and after the owner answers his last open question on the item,
  set it back: `agent` when the agent can continue, `none` when nothing
  waits. Keep `owner` only while another question for him on that item is
  still open.

  ```text
  toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent
  ```

- An item left at `owner` stays in the briefing and in
  `toolkit work decisions`, and `work-on` sends it to `work-decide` instead of
  its next stage.

## Stages in plain words

- Show a stage with the item id and the plain label from
  `toolkit work lifecycle`, for example "WI-012 is in testing (stage 09)".
- Never ask the owner which stage an item is in. Work it out from the record.
- Status follows the stage. `waiting_on` shows who the item is waiting for.
  Blocked is not a status.

## Owner edits win

The owner may edit the tracker by hand: move a folder, drag a Notion card,
change a stage. The CLI keeps his value, adds a "Changed by hand" history row,
and reports it. Never undo it. When a hand change skips a gate (a build item
moved past stage 03 without approved requirements, or Done without a recorded
result approval), ask the owner about it as a question.

## Branches and worktrees

- An item's code work happens on its own branch and worktree, named
  `wi-<number>-<slug>`, for example `wi-007-csv-export`. The briefing ties a
  worktree to its item by that name.
- Never commit `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. They are Git-ignored and live in
  the main checkout.
- No AI credit anywhere: not in commits, pull requests, comments, or files.
# Trackers

A project has exactly one tracker. `.toolkit.json` names it in
`tracker.type`. Read it with:

```text
toolkit config get tracker.type
```

| `tracker.type` | Where items live | How skills work with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | `.work-items/` in the main checkout, one folder per item | `toolkit work ...` commands |
| `notion` | The project's own Work Items database in Notion, under the "AI Agent Second Brain" page | `toolkit work ...` commands (the CLI calls Notion) |
| `github` | GitHub Issues in the project's repository | Written instructions: [trackers/github.md](trackers/github.md) |
| `jira` | Jira issues in the project's Jira project | Written instructions: [trackers/jira.md](trackers/jira.md) |

## Rules for every tracker

- The same model everywhere: the fourteen stages, the six statuses, the
  `WORK-ITEM.md` body, and one design per item. `toolkit work lifecycle`
  prints the stages, statuses, types, and approval gates.
- Never create a second tracker, and never keep a local copy of items that
  live in Notion, GitHub, or Jira.
- A sub-item is its own item with its own requirements, design, roadmap,
  and approvals. Finishing a sub-item never finishes or approves its parent.
- Only the main agent changes a work item. Agents return findings; the main
  agent saves them.
- Read every change back.

## Local and Notion

- Every read and write goes through `toolkit work ...`. The commands behave
  the same for both.
- Local: a folder nested inside an item's folder is a sub-item. A plain folder
  with no record in it is a group. `archive/` hides items from the briefing
  and from `toolkit work next`. The project's rule for this tracker is
  `.claude/rules/work-item-folders.md`.
- Notion: the design is the item's "Solution Design" child page. A card the
  owner made with Notion's New button has no template body; the CLI fills it
  on its next read and reports it. A Stage the owner changed by dragging is
  kept, and Status follows it.
- Writes outside the "AI Agent Second Brain" page are refused by the CLI.
  Never work around that.

## GitHub Issues and Jira

- `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3 and print the path of the written
  instructions. Follow those instructions instead.
- The work-item hooks do nothing for these trackers, so the skill must keep
  the item correct by itself: read it back after every change.
- Create nothing in GitHub or Jira that setup did not already approve (labels,
  fields, workflows). Creating and updating issues for work items is part of
  normal work once the tracker was chosen.

## Templates for every tracker

The templates come from the model project. The toolkit plugin carries an exact
copy of the model in its `scaffold/model/` folder, so every project can reach
them, whatever its tracker:

- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`: the work item
  body. A new GitHub issue body or Jira description starts from it, from
  `## Overview` to the end.
- `scaffold/model/.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md`: the design. A new
  design comment starts from it, without its frontmatter.

The file `~/.config/toolkit-v2/plugin-root` holds the path of the toolkit
plugin's folder (every session start refreshes it). The `scaffold/model/`
folder is inside that folder. A local project also has its own copies in
`.work-items/work-item-template/`, which the CLI prefers, so a project that
edited its template keeps its version. Both files open with a fill-in guide
comment: follow it, then delete it.

Statuses:
  Backlog      Logged; requirements are still being worked out (stages 01-02).
  Ready        Requirements approved; work can start (stage 03).
  In Progress  The item is active (stages 04-11). It does not mean building has started.
  In Review    The result is in a pull request, being deployed, or being written into the specifications (stages 12-14).
  Done         The owner accepted the result. Set only by toolkit work finish.
  Cancelled    Work stopped without the result. Set only by toolkit work cancel.

Types:
  discovery               Finding out what is needed.
  solution-design         Designing how something gets built.
  build                   Producing a change. Needs approved requirements before stage 03.
  data-load               Loading or changing data. Needs approved requirements before stage 03.
  repository-maintenance  Keeping the repository in order.
  research                Answering a question with sources.
  task                    A small piece of work.
  bug                     Something that does not work as it should.
  enhancement             An improvement to something that works.
  Other lower-case words are allowed as types.

Priorities: urgent, high, medium, low. Waiting on: owner, agent, external: <who>, none. Delivery: agent-led, owner-led, not-offered.

Approval gates:
  Requirements approval: asked by work-requirements; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <name>. build and data-load items cannot reach stage 03 or later without it. Sets stage 03 when the item is earlier.
  Design approval: asked by solution-design; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <name>. The design stays proposed until the owner approves it.
  Result approval (stage 11): asked by work-check; recorded with toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <name>. The owner approves the result before it is finished.
  Done: asked by work-finish; recorded with toolkit work finish <id> --by <name> --evidence <text>. Only this command sets Done. It records the result approval when none is recorded.
  Cancel: asked by work-finish; recorded with toolkit work cancel <id> --reason <text>. Only this command sets Cancelled. The reason is the owner's words.
  Delivery offer and team: asked by work-delegate; recorded with toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led|owner-led. Offered once per goal; the detail goes in Notes > Decisions and context.
  Project-wide decision: asked by work-decide; recorded with toolkit decision add --decision <text> --why <text> --by <name>. A row in DECISIONS.md at the project root.

What counts as approval:
  - Only the owner's explicit words count as approval. Quote them in the record.
  - A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer, or a saved draft is not approval.
  - Approval never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
  - Approval survives later stages. A stage alone does not prove approval: check the approval field.
  - A hand change that skips a gate is kept and reported as a question for the owner. It is never reverted.

Rules:
  - Status follows stage: 01-02 Backlog, 03 Ready, 04-11 In Progress, 12-14 In Review.
  - Stages may be skipped, repeated, and revisited. Record a one-line reason when a move is not obvious.
  - Pull-request stages (12) apply only to repository work.
  - Blocking is waiting_on plus the Overview Blockers line, never a status.
  - An item waiting on the owner continues with work-decide, whatever its stage.
  - An item that breaks an approval gate continues with work-decide until the owner answers.
  - An item at 11 User approval whose result approval is recorded continues with work-finish.

# Interviewing the owner and writing requirements

Detail for `work-requirements`. Carried over from Toolkit V1's requirements
interview, deep-interview, and spec-check rules, with V2 homes: everything
lands in the work item, not in a separate requirements document or notes file.

## Aim at the outcome the owner wants

- Work toward the outcome the owner wants, not only the words he used. Read a
  rough answer in the context of that requirement's purpose and the rest of
  the system, and ask focused follow-up questions until the real intent is
  clear.
- Say so when an answer would undermine his own goal, conflict with a stated
  constraint, cause a problem elsewhere, or when a clearly better approach
  exists. Name the concern, the tradeoff, and the direction you recommend,
  then let him choose. Once he has heard the concern and decided, do it his
  way.
- Never quietly replace what he said with what you inferred.
- Keep it light. Do not read every answer back for approval, do not challenge
  every answer, and do not start designing while the goal is still open.

## The interview

- Read the item, the related area file in `requirements/` (and
  `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md` when data is involved), the
  `system-guide/` file for the area, and memory before asking. Ask only what
  the records and the code cannot answer.
- One question at a time. Include a recommended answer based on what you
  know, so the owner can confirm, correct, or redirect it.
- Settle upstream decisions before the ones that depend on them.
- When the owner does not know, record an Open Questions row with who can
  answer, and continue with independent questions. Offer a `researcher` when
  a fact can be found.
- Follow contradictions and vague answers ("fast", "easy", "secure") until
  they are resolved or recorded as open questions.
- Save each settled answer into the item before asking the next question. A
  long interview fills the conversation; the item is the record that
  survives a cleared context.
- When resuming an interview, read the item first and continue from its
  Open Questions and Notes > Resume here.
- Near the end, ask: "What have we not touched that could change this?"

## Writing requirements someone else can use

- Plain words, no jargon. State the goal, what people must be able to do,
  what must happen, and the rules that govern it.
- Each requirement says what must be true and why, never how to build it. No
  file paths, versions, tool choices, or build steps in a requirement.
- Make behavior explicit: who is affected, when the rule applies, the
  expected result, and the exceptions. Include an observable acceptance
  check.
- Use only settled details. Leave missing decisions open as questions.
- Someone who was not in the conversation must be able to understand the
  goal, the required behavior, and how to tell it works.

`R-xx` block format (from the work-item template; the requirement name
follows an em dash, as in the template):

```markdown
#### R-01 — Rejected requests show their reason

**Status:** Refining  
**Applies to:** The person who submitted a request, after it is rejected.  
**Required behavior:** The requester can see the rejection reason on the request.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Requests withdrawn by the requester have no reason.  
**Acceptance check:** Reject a request with a reason; the requester sees that reason on the request.  
**Decision record:** Owner, 2026-09-26, interview.  
**Open questions:** None.
```

- Status words: Refining, Finalized, Superseded. The requirements approval
  command sets the Overall status; never write that line by hand. After the
  approval, set each approved `R-xx` to Finalized and add who approved it and
  when to its Decision record, in one section edit.
- A superseded requirement keeps its block, with Status Superseded and a link
  to the `R-xx` that replaced it.
- The Acceptance list says when the whole item can be accepted: the result,
  how it is checked, and any owner review.

## Build ideas

Ideas about how to build something go under Notes > Solution options and
considerations, linked to the `R-xx` they relate to. They are not
requirements and not an approved design. Example: "For R-01: a page message
or an email are possible ways to show the reason." Revisit these notes when a
requirement changes, so an old idea cannot quietly control the design.

## Corrections and changes

- Apply a clear correction without asking him to approve it again. Check the
  requirements and design it affects; ask only about consequences whose
  meaning is unclear.
- For a simple correction, acknowledge it in a sentence and ask only the next
  question that matters. Do not replay the whole item.
- A change to an approved requirement moves the item back to refinement and
  needs approval again. Keep the old wording in the decision record.
- After stage 03, say what the change affects: the design, tasks already
  built, sub-items.

## The spec check

Run it before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the
spec". Brief the `requirements-analyst` agent. It returns ready or not ready
and findings. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words: what to change,
where, and what the line would say instead.

- Change nothing without the owner's yes. Few findings: one decision at a
  time. Many: a short numbered list he can answer in one message.
- A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session.
- Two sources that disagree (the item and the area file in `requirements/`,
  for example): name both, quote the disagreement, and let the owner pick.
  Never silently prefer the newer or longer one.
- Do not turn the check into a rewrite. Personal wording taste is not a
  finding.
- Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Approval

- Show a short summary: the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the
  Acceptance list, and any open question.
- Ask exactly one line: "Do you approve these requirements?"
- Only his explicit yes counts. Quote it in the history note.
- After his yes: run the approval command, mark each approved `R-xx`
  Finalized with who approved it and when, and add the history note.
- Never approve while the Agreed goal is empty or a linked open question is
  still open.
- The owner asked for a design first: continue to `solution-design` with the
  open choices kept visible. That request is not a requirements approval.

# Decisions

Decisions for the whole project. A decision about one work item stays in that
item's Recent History. Add rows only with `toolkit decision add`, which gives
each row the next ID. Never rewrite an old row. To change a decision, add a new
row that names the ID it replaces.

| ID | Date | Decision | Why | Decided by | Replaces |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
---
paths:
  - "requirements/**"
  - "PROJECT-ROADMAP.md"
  - "PROJECT.md"
  - "DECISIONS.md"
  - "system-guide/**"
  - "tools/permissions/PERMISSIONS-RUNBOOK.md"
  - "ai-external-knowledge/**"
  - "delivery/**"
  - "**/README.md"
---
# Publish Project Documents

- In a copied Git repository, prepare each authorized documentation-only save in its own temporary Git worktree. Publish its commit directly to the default branch without a pull request.
- Rules, skills, hooks, prompts, settings, and code use a worktree and a pull request, even when written in Markdown.
- Saving a document does not approve its requirements or its build.
- Stage only this save's files, by name, in its worktree. Read the full staged diff.
- Never force-push or change another session's checkout. Resolve a remote advance in this save's worktree.
- An unpushed commit is unfinished. Verify the complete save reached the remote.
- Steps, checks, and recovery: the `publish-docs` skill.

- `.memory/` and `.work-items/` are local and Git-ignored. Their saves do not use this publication route.

/bin/zsh -lc "cat > /tmp/wi001-starting-request.txt <<'EOF'
Add a --version flag to the greet CLI. There is no greet CLI yet, so it has to be built too: a tiny Node.js tool where "'`node bin/greet.js Mike` prints `Hello, Mike!`.
EOF
cat > /tmp/wi001-active-requirements.txt <<'"'EOF'
#### R-01 — Greet the named person

**Status:** Refining  
**Applies to:** A person running the CLI with a name.  
**Required behavior:** The CLI prints "'`Hello, <name>!` for the supplied name.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Behavior for a missing name or additional arguments is unspecified.  
**Acceptance check:** Running `node bin/greet.js Mike` prints `Hello, Mike!` and a newline.  
**Decision record:** Owner request, 2026-09-27.  
**Open questions:** None.

#### R-02 — Show the tool version

**Status:** Refining  
**Applies to:** A person running the CLI with `--version`.  
**Required behavior:** The CLI prints the tool'"'s version and exits successfully.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** The initial version and exact output format need owner confirmation.  
**Acceptance check:** Running "'`node bin/greet.js --version` prints the declared version and a newline.  
**Decision record:** Owner request, 2026-09-27; version value and format proposed by agent.  
**Open questions:** Q-01.
EOF
cat > /tmp/wi001-acceptance.txt <<'"'EOF'
This work item can be accepted when:

1. The Node.js CLI greets "'`Mike` as `Hello, Mike!`.
2. `--version` prints the agreed version and exits successfully.
3. Automated checks and direct CLI runs confirm both commands, and the owner reviews the result.
EOF'

item.text:
I recorded the request as WI-001. The proposed behavior is: `node bin/greet.js Mike` prints `Hello, Mike!`, and `--version` prints the tool’s version.

What should the initial version be? I recommend `0.1.0`, printed as `0.1.0`. The project’s approval rule requires your answer and explicit requirements approval before I build the CLI.
